clue.text: 13 ac, sent off extremely excited

definitions.note: 13 across is ALL KEYED UP; this answer is a one-word equivalent

indicators.note: something that has gone off is spoilt, so the word beside it is no longer in its proper order
extremely points to the extremities of the next word, its first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Someone so wound up that they were sent off, as a footballer might be after losing their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cross-reference: 13 across is ALL KEYED UP, and TENSED means the same thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Being keyed up and being tensed are both states of nervous strain before some event, so the two answers are synonyms.

clue.text: See 2
Players in lamentable state traversing junction

indicators.note: to be in a state is to be agitated, so the letters before are thrown into disorder
traversing means crossing with, so the next item joins the letters already gathered

parts.note: a T-junction, so junction can be T

explanation.surface: A sports side in a sorry condition crossing a road junction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lamentable state' reads as one phrase, but lamentable is fodder and state the anagram signal. Netball is a team sport like basketball, hugely popular among women in Australia and Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A netball team is a group of seven people playing the game, so its members are players.

clue.text: Coming in last, after me, she gets caught

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so the following pieces go inside the word for last

parts.note: the end is the last part
taken as written; after me puts it second

explanation.surface: A woman arriving last, behind the speaker, gets nabbed.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas break the surface into a story about a latecomer; in fact 'after me, she' just fixes the order of the two pronouns before they go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To be enmeshed is to be caught in a net or mesh, literally or in a tangle of difficulties.

clue.text: Turned, moving like model empress

indicators.note: something turned is facing the other way, so the assembled letters are read from the end back to the start

parts.note: astir means up and moving about
the Model T Ford, so model can be T

explanation.surface: A model sashays down a catwalk, turning gracefully like an empress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' looks like a description of the model, but it applies to ASTIR+AS+T as a whole, which read backwards spells TSARITSA.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsaritsa was the wife of a Russian tsar, or a woman ruling in her own right, so she is an empress.

clue.text: Pole tends to be seen in hospitals

parts.note: a staff is a pole or stick
nurses means tends to, as a carer does

explanation.surface: A Polish patient being looked after in hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Pole is capitalised to suggest a person from Poland; it is a stick. The definition is descriptive rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Staff nurses are qualified, registered nurses on a ward, so they are people commonly found in hospitals.

clue.text: Allowance for leading seaman raised

indicators.note: in a down entry something raised is turned upward, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: leading is number one, No. 1, with the 1 as the letter I

explanation.surface: A senior sailor gets a pay rise in his allowance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leading seaman' is a real naval rank, so the phrase looks like one item; it splits into leading and seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: A ration is a fixed allowance of food or supplies issued to each person.

clue.text: Row about pre-tuned weapon

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for row is wrapped around the other piece

parts.note: a to-do is a row or fuss

indicators.note: tuned means adjusted, so the letters attached to it are rearranged

explanation.surface: An argument breaks out over a weapon tuned in advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pre-tuned' looks like one word, but splits into the fodder and its anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater missile, a naval weapon.

clue.text: Word puzzles incompetent actors — sic!

indicators.note: an incompetent job is botched, leaving the letters of the following words in a mess

explanation.surface: Bad actors are baffled by word puzzles, with sic noting the error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sic!' looks like an editor's note on the spelling, but its three letters belong in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrostic is a puzzle or poem in which the initial letters of lines spell a word.

clue.text: Time of year when nut turns to gold — around the fifth of November

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

indicators.note: a word that turns faces the other way, so the nut is read backwards
around says the turned word is wrapped about the letter that follows
the fifth of tells you to keep only the letter in fifth place of the next word

explanation.surface: Around Guy Fawkes Night the nuts and leaves turn golden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is the joining word putting gold after the reversed nut in the surface, but AU comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Autumn is one of the four seasons, which are times of the year.

clue.text: Job in fried fish shop for striker

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who coats the fish in batter
second meaning: someone who batters, that is, hits repeatedly

explanation.surface: A chip shop advertising a vacancy, apparently for someone who goes on strike.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition describes the worker rather than naming a job title, which is fair given the punning second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To batter is both to dip fish in a flour-and-egg coating and to beat someone, so a batterer does either.

clue.text: Bloomers that drive men mad?

parts.note: surface reading: women's baggy knickers, the kind that might inflame a man; setter's reading: plants that bloom, named after strong emotion

explanation.surface: A saucy picture of underwear driving men wild.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomers are knickers on the surface but simply flowering plants here; 'drive men mad' hints at passion, which names the climbing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Passion flowers are climbing plants with showy blooms, and passion is the feeling that drives people mad.

clue.text: A pure oboe arrangement incorporating a double forte composed for performance on stage

definitions.note: a description of a stage work rather than a noun synonym

indicators.note: a musical arrangement reworks the material, so the letters of these words are rearranged

parts.note: ff, fortissimo, is forte doubled in musical notation

explanation.surface: A musical score: an oboe arrangement with a loud passage, written for the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: In musical notation f is forte (loud), so a double forte is ff. Both pieces go into the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Opera bouffe is French comic opera, a work written to be staged.

clue.text: Nerves taut, Luke played rather badly

definitions.note: a noun phrase describing the state; the answer is the adjective for it

indicators.note: something performed rather badly comes out jumbled, so the letters are set down in a muddled order

explanation.surface: A nervous musician called Luke gives a poor performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'played' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder; 'rather badly' does that job.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone keyed up is tense with nervous anticipation, which is what taut nerves describe.

clue.text: One country makes a small investment in another

indicators.note: an investment is something put into a thing, so these letters go inside the other country

explanation.surface: One nation puts a little money into another.
explanation.walkthrough: A and L go inside Austria. L for small is loose (it usually means large or learner), but the crossings and definition fix the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Australia is a nation, home of the newspaper that printed this puzzle.

clue.text: A swamp retreats to reveal desert

indicators.note: something that retreats goes backwards, so these letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a, as in one, which is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A drought makes the marshland shrink back to bare desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' standing for one and so for I is the trick; read I BOG backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gobi is a vast desert in Mongolia and northern China.

clue.text: Begging to take tea out in lobby

definitions.note: a noun here: the act of begging, a plea

indicators.note: in places the shuffled letters inside the word for lobby

parts.note: an entry is an entrance hall or lobby

indicators.note: out suggests the word is put out of order, so its letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: Someone pleads to be allowed to take their tea out into the foyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take tea out' sounds like carrying a cup away, but out reshuffles tea and in puts the result inside the lobby.
explanation.definitionFit: An entreaty is an earnest request or plea, which is what begging means as a noun.

clue.text: Warships advance south

parts.note: a sub is an advance on wages
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A fleet steams forward towards the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'advance' reads as a verb for the fleet but is a noun: a sub is money paid ahead of wages.
explanation.definitionFit: Subs is short for submarines, naval vessels that count as warships.

clue.text: Stage kiss best!

parts.note: buss is an old word for kiss

explanation.surface: A theatre critic praising an on-stage kiss as the best.
explanation.walkthrough: Stage reads as the theatre, but it means a stopping point on a bus route, as in a fare stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus stop is a point on a route where passengers board, which is what a fare stage marks.

clue.text: Aliases used by footballers at college means trouble

parts.note: the FA is the Football Association

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so the word before is stirred into a new order

parts.note: the LSE is the London School of Economics

explanation.surface: Student footballers using made-up names is bound to lead to trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'means trouble' reads as a phrase, but means is the fodder and trouble a verb signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An alias is an assumed name, so aliases are false names used to hide one's identity.

clue.text: Where doctor gets over sunburn in North America?

indicators.note: in places the sunburn letters inside the abbreviation for the continent
in a down entry over means on top, so the doctor's letters sit above the rest

parts.note: a tan is what the sun leaves on skin

explanation.surface: A question about where in North America a doctor might deal with sunburn.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is just 'Where', fair because the answer is a place; the question mark covers it.
explanation.definitionFit: Montana is a US state, so it answers 'where' as a location in North America.

clue.text: Some start further down — and further back?

indicators.note: start points to the beginning of the word before, keeping only its opening letter

explanation.surface: A race with a staggered start where some runners begin further down the track.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition: in a race the slower runner ends up further back.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone slower than the rest falls behind, so they are further back in the field.

clue.text: Piano piece rewritten for lutes — well!

indicators.note: a text that is rewritten comes out in a new form, so the following words are rearranged

parts.note: a spring is a well, a source of water

explanation.surface: Someone is pleasantly surprised to hear a piano work arranged for lutes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well!' looks like an exclamation of surprise, but it is a noun meaning a spring. The piece is by the Norwegian composer Christian Sinding.
explanation.definitionFit: Rustle of Spring is a popular short piano work by Sinding, a staple of parlour pianists.

clue.text: Popular expression of public feeling somewhat undemocratic

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of the next word is wanted, a run of letters inside it

parts.note: letters three to six of the word

explanation.surface: A street protest that some think is a little undemocratic.
explanation.definitionFit: A demo, short for demonstration, is a public protest by a crowd voicing shared feeling.

clue.text: Biblical character of Spooner's query concerning existence?

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words are exchanged

parts.note: a question about existence; swap the opening sounds of its two words

explanation.surface: A biblical figure asking a philosophical question about the meaning of life.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the W and L sounds turns the question into the name of a woman from Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: Lot's wife appears in Genesis, turned into a pillar of salt for looking back at Sodom.

clue.text: Friend — expert at building luxury home

indicators.note: building means putting parts together, so one piece is set after the other

explanation.surface: A friend who is a skilled builder puts up a mansion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'expert at building' reads as one skilled tradesman, but building signals assembling the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A palace is a grand residence, the most luxurious kind of home.

clue.text: Spiritually moved?

parts.note: surface reading: emotionally or religiously stirred; setter's reading: physically carried by spirits, as at a seance

explanation.surface: Someone deeply touched by a religious experience.
explanation.walkthrough: In spiritualism an apport is an object said to be brought into a seance by spirits; the question mark flags this literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiritualists say spirits transport objects to a seance; an object so transported has been carried by spirit agency.

clue.text: Monday's fireball?

indicators.note: the question mark warns that the day's name is not meant literally and its letters must be reordered

explanation.surface: A meteor seen at the start of the week.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram word: the question mark alone signals that the letters of the weekday are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A fireball is an energetic, forceful person, and so is a dynamo, a figurative use of the generator.
